box.text: In C, every variable is a box in memory... and every box has an address.

n.text: Here, n holds forty-two. And ampersand n? That's the address of that box.

pointer.text: [curious] So what's a pointer? It's just a variable that holds an address. Int star p, set to ampersand n, stores where n lives.

star.text: Star p goes to that address. Reading star p gives you forty-two, and writing one hundred through it changes n ITSELF.

sizes.text: On this machine, an int takes four bytes, and a pointer takes eight. The addresses change on every run, but p always holds the address of n.

trap.text: Now, here's the classic trap. This swap takes two ints and trades them.

copies.text: But C passes copies. So swap gets two new boxes, a and b, holding one and two.

nothing.text: The copies trade... and x and y? They stay exactly as they were.

fix.text: So, pass the addresses instead. Call swap with ampersand x and ampersand y, and a and b now hold where x and y live.

works.text: Now star a and star b reach back into main's boxes, so x and y REALLY trade.

rule.text: And that's all a pointer is. Ampersand asks where a variable lives, and star goes there.
